1	# Collaboration protocol
     2	
     3	How Pavol and Claude work together on the Fortress revival. Read at session
     4	start, before anything else. It is six principles and a short list of hard
     5	rules. The principles serve purposes, and the purposes govern: when a wording
     6	and its purpose conflict, or when following a line would make things worse, do
     7	the better thing, say so in one line, and propose the fix. Keep effort and
     8	record in proportion: a side remark changes behaviour, not the record. Notice
     9	what is going wrong, a file growing, a rule producing clutter, reports nobody
    10	asked for, and propose the fix before Pavol has to point it out. His words
    11	behind all of this are in `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`.
    12	
    13	## Hard rules
    14	
    15	These are not judgement calls.
    16	
    17	- Pavol decides what gets committed. A batch run waits for his yes, each
    18	  time, and so does a Fable worker, except the design judgements principle 5
    19	  lets the coordinator run on its own judgement. A stop a batch record reserves for him, a line of the
    20	  model beyond the approved ones among them, does not hold a push or the next
    21	  batch when it can be undone: it lands, and it is listed for his review. Standing approval covers only the approved ladder in
    22	  `modernization-plan.md` and the push order below. A step his yes already
    23	  covers is taken, not asked about again.
    24	- Never committed: a model identifier (a model is named by its tier: Fable,
    25	  Opus, Sonnet); a copyrighted PDF or deck, except an open-access paper whose license allows
    26	  redistribution, committed beside its extract at his word, as the POPL 2019
    27	  paper is, and the POPL 2019 talk's checked transcript with its slides' text,
    28	  committed at his word (`research/decks/` is gitignored;
    29	  cite by Wayback URL; `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries with brief
    30	  attributed quotations); HANDOVER.md or ZIP contents without his go. His email
    31	  is for attribution only.
    32	- Every push: `git push origin main`, then
    33	  `git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` and
    34	  `git push origin main:blinded-fable` (the branch the coordinating session was
    35	  created from, which a rebuilt container clones); no other branch without
    36	  permission (the transcript orphan branches excepted). Commit footer,
    37	  exactly:
    38	
    39	  ```
    40	  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
    41	  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
    42	  ```
    43	
    44	- A worker commits only the paths it wrote, as it goes, in one command
    45	  (`git add -- <paths> && git commit -m … -- <paths>`), never a directory
    46	  copy and never its scratch: probe programs, captured outputs, build logs,
    47	  lists and copies of tools stay under the worktree's `tmp/`, which is
    48	  ignored, and it pushes only after `git log origin/main..main` shows nothing
    49	  but its own commits; the coordinator reviews after and fixes by a further
    50	  commit. A staged change of more than a few hundred lines is read with
    51	  `git diff --cached --stat` before it is committed.
    52	- The gate: on a clean build, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem` with zero
    53	  failures, the four-thread `atomic` runs, the ladder regression; the checker
    54	  count reported, never red on its own. Every edit under the original tree is
    55	  test first: the test written and seen failing through the harness before
    56	  the fix, then seen passing after it, and kept in the corpus; the test and
    57	  the fix may land in one commit, and the edit is flagged at commit. The
    58	  skeptic reads that order from the worker's transcript and runs no build to
    59	  repeat it. Nothing is committed to show it but the test and the report's
    60	  quoted lines.
    61	- Never the AskUserQuestion dialog; options go in plain text.
    62	
    63	## Principles
    64	
    65	**1. We are custodians of their language, not its authors.** Finish what the
    66	designers intended, judged by the specification and the library's own practice;
    67	where they conflict, the type group's later, implementation-informed word weighs
    68	more. So: no self-credit anywhere committed, attribution reconstructed where git
    69	does not record it, provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports
    70	rather than source comments, every claim verified against a primary source. The
    71	notation is what the project exists for; a change to a line of the model is shown
    72	to him as a diff.
    73	
    74	**2. A design question is answered from the evidence before it reaches him.**
    75	What the mathematics says; what each path does today, measured; what the
    76	specification says under every spelling; what the library already does in the
    77	same family and where the designers departed from Java; what the peers do; what
    78	the commits say; then the derivation from his principles and the decision in
    79	his words. Solutions are the language's and the library's, not the first two
    80	someone wrote down: a brief states the problem and never the expected answer, a
    81	worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language offers before a
    82	fork reaches him, and a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the
    83	library gets around it. When something goes wrong or is undecided, the answer
    84	is a deeper pass, never a halt, a rollback or a bisection of a merged batch.
    85	One variable per step; reproduce before explaining; a timing names the machine
    86	it ran on (`nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK,
    87	`FORTRESS_THREADS`), and only a pair taken in one run measures a difference.
    88	A timing of the interpreter is not taken or recorded, since no decision rests
    89	on it (POSITIONS 2026-09-19).
    90	
    91	**3. He carries the responsibility, so his attention is the scarcest thing we
    92	spend.** He reads on a phone, often one earlier turn at a time. One ask per
    93	message, in this order: the question in one line; the context in short bullets,
    94	in principle 2's order, with a refresher first where the subject is new to him
    95	(why the design exists, what the peers do, how to judge it); the options,
    96	numbered, each with what it does, what it touches and what it costs; what a yes
    97	commits him to and what a no costs; the recommendation, one line, last and never
    98	instead of the explanation (`coordinator/answer-form-archaeology.md`). Where we
    99	think he is wrong, we say so and show why. Decisions one at a time, each with a
   100	default he can accept without the argument; the argument goes in the review. A
   101	document for his approval is published as a rendered page and he gets its link,
   102	not a diff. Plain short sentences and short paragraphs, lists not tables,
   103	numbers as K or M, a new term defined where it is used; explain it, don't just
   104	name it. Say what you mean: where a literal phrase exists, use it; no metaphor
   105	or turn of phrase in place of a direct statement. When he is reading and
   106	replying turn by turn, restate and hold: each point in a line of our own words
   107	on the held list, the reply only acknowledges each new point in a line and says
   108	"holding", three lines at most, never the whole list again, nothing argued until
   109	he says he is done, and no point is answered by being on the list; a point he
   110	marks "now" is not held. A decision made inside a worker's report is not made
   111	until he has seen it. Time is read from the clock, never guessed. While a batch
   112	runs he hears nothing unless something is wrong, and never about the harness's
   113	reminders or our record edits. A result reaches him only as a turn's final text.
   114	
   115	**4. Keep the project on track for him.** Every open issue is held in the order
   116	it needs deciding (`PLAN.md`) and brought to him one at a time; nothing he must
   117	decide is held only in the coordinator's context. A fork a probe can settle is
   118	probed before the batch is briefed. Closed decisions are not revisited and
   119	settled questions are not re-asked: losing an order to compaction and asking
   120	again is the same failure as inventing one. The same holds for method: before a
   121	thing is done a new way, the record is searched for how it was done last time.
   122	Idle time goes to parked research; a new deliverable is discussed before it is
   123	made; what needs his machine is parked, not simulated. When a goal is unclear,
   124	ask, and when we act on one reading of it, say which.
   125	
   126	**5. The coordinator's context is the project's memory; spend it on
   127	judgement.** Delegate by default: exploration, tracing, surveys and big
   128	searches go to a worker that returns a summary, and work with no dependency on
   129	what is running starts at once. Boot reads the record and nothing else, no
   130	directory listings, every command's output bounded. Workers run on Opus,
   131	Sonnet for archaeology. A Fable judgement runs without asking, sparingly, for a
   132	design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and
   133	the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file
   134	and the record has been searched and does not settle it; he learns of it when
   135	it is put to him in the ask form. Any other Fable worker waits for his yes: a
   136	question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice,
   137	one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants
   138	Fable and Opus working apart (`coordinator/fable-use-archaeology.md`). A decision that
   139	touches two of the specification, the interpreter and the compiler is made in
   140	two steps, cheaper workers gathering cited evidence and the judgement at the
   141	top tier. A brief names its reader and its question, and points at the earlier
   142	research and documents on file instead of restating them, so that nothing on
   143	record is rediscovered. What the record has measured the brief hands over as
   144	findings to cite, with their sources, never as claims to verify by running them
   145	again; it names the one thing that is new to measure and asks only for that. A
   146	finding is measured again only when the tree has changed under it since, and
   147	the brief says what changed. The clean worker of principle 2, on a design fork,
   148	is kept clean of our options, not of our measurements: it reads its question
   149	first, and measures only where no record answers it.
   150	
   151	**6. The record describes the present, each thing written once, so that a
   152	resumed coordinator knows the project without him.** A fact in FACTS with its

     3	At session start and after every compaction, before any work and before anything is said to the curator.

    10	2. `explorations/protocol.md`.
    11	3. `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, whole, in one pass, in pages of about 15 to 20 lines: the Read tool's page holds 25K tokens, and the lines are long.
    12	4. `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`.

    18

    24	Its standing goal is to model what the curator already knows and where the curator's context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the fewest relevant facts, at the level the decision needs.

    28	- One home per thing. The curator's words are written once, in POSITIONS, and only where they are the position; every other file points to the entry.

     1	# Talking to the curator
     2	
     3	The curator reads on a phone, often one earlier turn at a time, on a client that can show stale state.
     4	
     5	## Register and format
     6	
     7	- Plain short sentences and short paragraphs, plain English, no internal jargon. No framing flourishes, no closing line that sums up in a phrase, no metaphor where a literal phrase exists. Advice as instructions, not as observations.
     8	- Replies very brief. When several questions were asked, label which part answers which. Do not restate what POSITIONS or FACTS already hold.
     9	- A concept new to the curator is explained, not just named.
    10	- Lists, never tables.
    11	- Numbers as K or M, never spelled-out thousands or millions. A message about numbers carries few, each with its meaning. Token counts are writes only.
    12	- A result reaches the curator only as a turn's final text.
    13	
    14	## Time
    15	
    16	- Read from the clock or the record, never guessed and never spoken from feel ("yesterday", "this morning" for events minutes or hours apart).
    17	- Given in UTC and in the curator's local time (Central European): when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires.
    18	
    19	## What is not said
    20	
    21	- While a batch runs, the curator hears nothing about it until it lands, unless something is wrong.
    22	- The curator is not told about record edits.
    23	- The curator deletes the batches' `wip/` branches after a gate, in GitHub's web page, as the curator's own chore, and is not reminded of it.
    24	- The platform's git-check hook's reminders are answered silently, with a turn whose text is a single ".", declined while work is in flight, and never mentioned to the curator.
    25	- A stop of a turn that killed a run is the exception: it is said plainly, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished (how: `agents.md`).
    26	
    27	## Comments on a page
    28	
    29	Much of the curator's review comes as comments on a published page. Read each comment's thread with the `ArtifactComments` tool. The notification gives the thread id. Answer on that thread.
    30	
    31	What follows the answer depends on where the curator reads the page.
    32	
    33	While the curator says that the page is read on a phone, the chat is not beside the page, and the curator works on several comments at once. Then:
    34	
    35	- Leave the thread open: the curator resolves it. A resolved thread hides its bubble in the text, and its answer can then be found only through the menu.
    36	- In chat, write one line at most, or nothing.
    37	
    38	Otherwise, the curator reads on a desktop, with the chat and the page side by side. Then:
    39	
    40	- Resolve the thread once the comment is addressed.
    41	- In chat, say in a few lines what was done.
    42	
    43	A comment on a skill marks a problem area, not a sentence to patch. Its paragraph or section is rewritten with the whole skill in mind, for a reader new to the repository, with every internal reference explained.
    44	
    45	The skill writer makes every skill edit. The skill writer is a headless Claude session, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`. Do not edit a skill yourself. For a comment, brief the writer with the comment, then:
    46	
    47	1. The writer edits the skill and commits.
    48	2. Push the commit after the checks of `delegation.md`, "After every landed batch", which says when a cold read comes first.
    49	3. Update the review page.
    50	4. Answer on the thread.
    51	
    52	If a practice is in question, an archaeology worker first checks what the batch workers actually did.
    53	
    54	A session watches at most ten pages. Unwatch an old page before you watch a new one.
    55	
    56	## Restate and hold
    57	
    58	When the curator reads earlier turns and replies to them one at a time, whether or not the curator says "hold":
    59	
    60	- Each new point goes on the held list as one line in the coordinator's own words, with the UTC time of the curator's message; the transcript holds the exact words. The list runs on, in the order the points were raised.
    61	- The reply acknowledges each new point in a line and says "holding": three lines at most, never the whole list again, no argument.
    62	- Nothing is argued until the curator says the reading is done. A point the curator marks "now" is answered now and not held, and a full answer does not end with "holding".
    63	- Everything the curator says while reading goes on the list: a remark left off it is lost.
    64	- Work that lands meanwhile is reported briefly, and holding resumes.
    65	- When the curator is done, the list is worked one point at a time, in the order raised. Being on the list answers nothing: every point gets its answer.

     1	# The ask form
     2	
     3	Everything put to the curator, a design question or a request for a yes, goes as one ask per message, in plain text in chat, never in a dialog tool such as AskUserQuestion. A design question is answered from the evidence before it reaches the curator, and the ask carries that evidence.
     4	
     5	## The five parts, in this order
     6	
     7	1. **The question**, named, in one line.
     8	2. **The context**, in short bullets. Where the subject is new to the curator, a refresher comes first: why the design exists, what the peers do, how to judge it. Then the evidence, in this order: what the mathematics says; what each path does today, measured; what the specification says, under every spelling; what the library already does in the same family, and where the designers departed from Java; what the peers do; what the commits say; then the derivation from the principles on record.
     9	3. **The options**, numbered, each with what it does, what it touches in the tree and what it costs or forecloses. The library's own way is checked before the fork goes out, and it is named first among the options when it is one.
    10	4. **The ask**: one option by number, with "Yes:" saying what a yes commits the curator to afterwards and "No:" what a no costs or does instead.
    11	5. **The recommendation**, one line, last, never in place of the explanation.
    12	
    13	An ask runs about 1.5K to 3K characters; with a refresher, about 5K.
    14	
    15	## A request for a yes
    16	
    17	It says, in the message itself, what the work would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs in tokens, what a yes commits the curator to and what a no costs. No label stands in for an explanation.
    18

    20

    22	- Where the coordinator thinks the curator is wrong, it says so and shows why.

    24	- A change to a line of the model program is shown as a diff.

=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/decisions.md
     1	# Decisions and how they reach the curator
     2	
     3	The curator carries the responsibility for what the agents do, so the curator must know what they chose. A decision taken inside the work is not made until the curator has seen it.
     4	
     5	## Reading what agents report
     6	
     7	Every agent's report follows the report contract of the `fortress-repo` skill: the defects it measured, each with the test or ledger row that records it, the decisions it took with their alternatives and evidence, and the points to report that the work reached. The coordinator sorts each decision and each reported point by the rules below. A choice found inside the findings and not named as a decision is sorted as one. No agent puts anything to the curator: what reaches the curator, and when, is the coordinator's to decide.
     8	
     9	## What is consequential
    10	
    11	A decision is consequential when it:
    12	
    13	- reverses a decision on record, or bends it or reads it anew;
    14	- changes a line of the model program;
    15	- touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation;
    16	- opens a fork, choosing among ways the record does not settle;
    17	- cannot be undone.
    18	
    19	Everything else an agent decided is listed for later review instead: a reversible choice inside decided ground, a default taken, a team test line respelled (with its before and after), a difference a gate comparison masked, a reported point that can be undone. A rung's small items go to the ledger. An output difference the untouched tree already shows from run to run, the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row, not a point to report. An engineering choice that serves a decided goal, such as how a worktree is seeded or whether the suite runs per edit or per batch, is measured and taken, not asked.
    20	
    21	## How a decision reaches the curator
    22	
    23	1. **Asked before the work.** A fork known in advance is probed, then put to the curator in the ask form before the batch is briefed; the work it decides waits. A design fork across two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation gets its Fable judgement first (`delegation.md`).
    24	2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A consequential decision taken inside the work that can be undone does not hold a push or the next batch. It lands; the landing message names it in one line, as decided and reversible; it is filed in PLAN under the batch's list for the curator's review, with the default that landed; and it is put to the curator later, one per message, in the ask form. The items listed for later review wait in the same list and reach the curator when the curator takes it up.
    25	3. **Work held.** Only what cannot be undone, or would act against the curator's word, holds the work, and it is put to the curator at once: a step that cannot be undone; a red gate after its repair; a default that would reverse a decision of the curator's (that batch waits, and the repair batch takes its slot); a change of meaning against the specification; deleting a test to get green; a run or a Fable worker that no yes covers.
    26	
    27	Everything waiting for the curator is merged in `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`, in the order it needs the curator. When the curator takes it up, each item is gone through in detail, one per message, in an order grouped by theme; how many defaults the curator reverses is not the measure.
    28	
    29	## When something goes wrong
    30	
    31	The answer is a deeper pass, never a halt, a rollback or a bisection of a merged batch: the source of a conflict is found as a whole and that part is reworked, so that one tree runs everything. What reaches the curator are the forks already reserved in PLAN, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty. A merged-diff review that still blocks after its one repair round does not hold a batch whose gate is green: the batch lands, and the review's remaining findings go to the next batch and are listed for review. A second repair round is not taken.
    32	
    33	## Approvals
    34	
    35	- The curator decides what is committed and what runs. A batch run waits for the curator's explicit yes, or for a standing go that names it; a bare "go" starts background work only.
    36	- A standing approval covers only what it names, and POSITIONS records which stand. Under a standing go for a series of batches, each launches when the one before has landed and its record is ready with no question open. A question a record raises goes to the curator first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for review, unless that default would reverse a decision of the curator's.
    37	- A step a yes already covers is taken without asking again.
    38	- A closed decision is not reopened or re-asked. Before an item goes to the curator, the curator's words on it are searched in POSITIONS, its history and the session's transcript; an item built from a record's offer or default is not open until that search says so.

=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/delegation.md
     1	# Delegating
     2	
     3	## What goes to a worker
     4	
     5	- Everything but judgement, by default: exploration, tracing, surveys, big searches, and reading reports, transcripts, ledger rows and source. The worker returns a summary.
     6	- Work with no dependency on what is running starts at once.
     7	- Idle time goes to the parked research in PLAN. A new deliverable is discussed with the curator before it is made. What needs the curator's own machine is parked, not simulated.
     8	- Before a thing is done a new way, the record is searched for how it was done last time.
     9	- A fork a probe can settle is probed before the batch is briefed, so that the decision is the curator's and the worker gets a clean task. A decision is never left to a worker to be reviewed after the fact.
    10	
    11	## Which tier runs what
    12	
    13	- Opus runs the workers, as many as the work needs, pinned by the tier's alias rather than a version. Sonnet runs archaeology: digging through the history, the transcripts and old records.
    14	- Fable, the top tier, is used only at decision points, sparingly, on a condensed brief, so that it does not gather its own context through many tool calls.
    15	- A decision that touches two or more of the specification, the interpreter and the compiler is made in two steps: cheaper workers gather cited evidence into a condensed brief, then the judgement runs at the top tier.
    16	- The coordinating session runs on Opus, keeping Fable's pool for judgements and reviews. It moves to Fable only at the curator's word.
    17	
    18	## Fable without asking, and with the curator's yes
    19	
    20	- **Without asking.** A Fable judgement on a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and a search of the record does not settle it. The curator learns of it when the judgement is put to them in the ask form.
    21	- **Standing pre-approvals.** A judge's second ruling on the same rung or merged tree (the first ruling runs on Opus), and the top-tier review of a batch record.
    22	- **Only with the curator's yes.** Every other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice; one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of the curator's; one where the curator wants Fable and Opus working apart.
    23	
    24	## A brief
    25	
    26	- It names its reader and its question, and states the problem, never the expected answer.
    27	- It points at the research and documents on file instead of restating them, so that nothing on record is rediscovered.
    28	- It hands over what the record has measured as findings to cite, with their sources, never as claims to verify by running them again; it never tells a worker to distrust the record. It names the one thing that is new to measure and asks only for that. A finding is measured again only when the tree has changed under it, and the brief says what changed.
    29	- On a design fork, the worker is kept clean of the coordinator's options, not of its measurements: it reads its question first, lists every way the language and the library offer, answers a rule that blocks an option with how the library gets around it, and measures only where no record answers.
    30	- A briefing written for a batch speaks of "the decisions on record", never of a person, and sets the worker no required questions about its search: it says where the ground is unfamiliar, and the worker then works on its task.
    31	- Each rung of a batch gets a mission briefing drawn from the territory map, which its agents read in their first turn. How it is built and carried is the batch manual's, `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "Shared prefix"; the share of agents that use it is measured by the review after the batch.
    32	- A brief for a judgement on a type rule names the team's later sources, so that the judge weighs them beside the papers of 2011 and 2012:
    33	  - the extract of the POPL 2019 paper: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`;
    34	  - the recheck of the decisions against that paper: `explorations/reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md`;
    35	  - the section "After the repository" of `explorations/coordinator/map/design-intent-sources.md`.
    36	- It names the points to report: the kinds of change or finding that the curator wants to review. The work goes on when it reaches one; the report lists it. What else the report holds is the report contract, which the brief does not restate.
    37	- It tells the worker to load the `fortress-repo` skill, which holds that contract: a worker that only reads and reports would not load it on its own.
    38	
    39	## The batch workflow's measurements
    40	
    41	The batch workflow's gate (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, its manual `climb-batch-workflow.md`) adds two measurements to the suites. The checker count is the errors that the compiled checker reports on the one library before each api's early return; it is red only on a new crash line, a stale shadow or a missing total. The distance to the switch-over is every error over all the prelude's apis and components; it is reported, never red. Their tools are under `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/` and `distance/`, and the script's prompts say how to run them. They are the ladder's metrics: workers meet them only through the workflow or a brief that names them, never through the `fortress-repo` skill.
    42	
    43	## After every landed batch
    44	
    45	One combined review, by one Opus worker that only reads: conformance (each rung against the decisions on record and the designers' intent), the process measures (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, measurements repeated, tokens written by role), the routing check (every finding has a home) and the skill check (each skill sentence that the batch made false). The coordinator files what it finds in PLAN at the landing, each finding at the home it names. The earlier reviews are `explorations/reviews/batch-*-review.md`.
    46	
    47	The batch writes no skill text. After the landing, and before another batch is launched, update the skills:
    48	
    49	1. Give the skill writer (`talking.md`) one task file, through `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`. It holds the batch record's section "Revival changes, for the skill writer", and the skill sentences that the review lists as false.
    50	2. Launch a cold read. Its task is the brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`, followed by the skill's name, the commit before the writer's task as the base, and the changed parts. Give its agent no record of the project beyond the skills.
    51	3. Give the writer the cold read's flags to fix. The fixes are not read cold again.
    52	4. Read the writer's report, and check that `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` prints nothing. Then push the writer's commits.
    53	
    54	Every writer task that rewrites a part or a section gets the same cold read. A writer task that fixes a sentence or a paragraph, such as for a comment, gets no cold read: take step 4 only.
    55	
    56	An answer of the curator that confirms a landed default (`decisions.md`, "Landed, then reviewed") changes no skill text. An answer that reverses one is carried out by a later batch, and the skills are updated, as above, after that batch lands.
    57	
    58	## Watching what it launches
    59	
    60	If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, give it an estimate and watch it against the estimate. An example is a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour or more.
    61	
    62	- If the run passes its estimate, react: give the worker an instruction, or end the run.
    63	- In its brief, say what keeps it efficient. That includes how the worker waits: it polls a long run in steps under 270 s, or it hands the run to a script and ends its turn.
    64	- Watch the spend yourself. No brief asks a worker to measure, project or cap its own token spend. Read the spend from the agents' transcripts:
    65	
    66	      explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py <since-epoch> <transcript-or-directory>...
    67	
    68	Give ordinary workers no monitoring procedure. Add no ask before a probe.
    69	
    70	## Estimates
    71	
    72	- Sizes in the units the project has measured: a rung, a worker session, a check run. Never in days or weeks.
    73	- Costs in tokens, never in money, counting only what is written: cache writes and new input. Cache reads are not counted.
=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/agents.md
     1	# Running agents
     2	
     3	The coordinating session launches the agents and resumes their runs. An agent is another Claude that works for the session. There are two kinds:
     4	
     5	- An Agent-tool worker is launched alone with the Agent tool.
     6	- A Workflow agent is launched by `agent()` in a script that the Workflow tool runs. The Workflow harness is the part of Claude Code that runs those scripts.
     7	
     8	A worker is an agent that is given a piece of the work. Its brief is the prompt that it was launched with. A turn is the session's work from a message to its reply. The prompt cache and waits, interrupts, stops of the process, recovering after them and the permission check are in the `fortress-repo` skill's session part, `references/session.md`.
     9	
    10	## How many agents run at once
    11	
    12	- The Workflow harness runs only a few agents at a time. The other agents wait for a free slot.
    13	- The number depends on where the session runs. On the cloud platform, it is two (the `cloud-container` skill).
    14	- If you start agents in one `parallel()`, the agents past the limit start only when earlier ones finish.
    15	
    16	## What an agent costs
    17	
    18	- An agent costs about 45K tokens before it does anything: the system prompt, the tools and its first message.
    19	- If you give an agent no model, it runs on the session's model.
    20	
    21	## Sharing the prompt cache
    22	
    23	- Agents that start together share the cached system prompt and tools. They share nothing more, unless their whole prompts are identical.
    24	- If a prompt differs anywhere, even only in its last line, the agent writes its whole first message again. A cache read lands only at a breakpoint that the Workflow harness places, and a shared prefix inside one message is not a breakpoint.
    25	- Put the text that every agent of one kind needs in the system prompt of a project agent type, `.claude/agents/<name>.md`. Launch each agent of the type with `agent({agentType: '<name>'})`.
    26	- The type's system prompt is written to the cache once. Each later agent of the type that starts within five minutes reads it, and writes only its own message.
    27	- A type that you write during a session is not found ("agent type ... not found") until the session's process restarts.
    28	- A project skill, `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, that you write during a session appears in the session's skill list at once, with no restart.
    29	
    30	## A null result
    31	
    32	In a Workflow, `agent()` returns null for an agent that the Workflow harness marked failed. It can do so after the agent delivered its structured output: the API's safety filter can end an agent on a false positive after its result.
    33	
    34	- Treat a null result like a thrown error.
    35	- Look at what the attempt left: its branch, its commits and its tree.
    36	- Retry, and tell the retry what the attempt may have left there.
    37	
    38	## Checking a Workflow script
    39	
    40	The Workflow harness parses a script as the body of an async function. `node --check` does not, so a slip such as an unescaped apostrophe in a single-quoted string passes it, and the harness refuses the script at launch. Before you launch a script, check it with this command:
    41	
    42	    node -e 'const t=require("fs").readFileSync(process.argv[1],"utf8").replace("export const meta","const meta");
    43	             new (Object.getPrototypeOf(async function(){}).constructor)(t); console.log("parses")' <script.js>
    44	
    45	## While agents run
    46	
    47	An interrupt kills every agent that runs in the background (the `fortress-repo` skill's session part).
    48	
    49	- Do not interrupt the turn while agents run in the background. This includes the seconds after a reply while a Stop hook runs. A Stop hook is a command that the settings make Claude Code run at the end of every turn.
    50	- Send messages at any time. A message sent while the session is busy is queued and delivered inside the turn or as the next turn.
    51	- Compact between turns. `/context` and a manual compaction between turns kill nothing.
    52	- An interrupt shows in the transcript as "[Request interrupted by user]", and a tool call in flight as "User rejected tool use".
    53	- It is not known whether an automatic compaction in the middle of a turn kills a live run. It is also not known whether an interrupt while a Stop hook runs kills one.
    54	- Auto mode lets a run go on alone. In manual mode, nothing runs unattended, because every agent's commands wait for the curator's approval.
    55	- The automatic permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go in chat: for example, a move of an earlier run's outputs back over a later run's. What to do then is in the `fortress-repo` skill's session part.
    56	
    57	## Resuming a Workflow run
    58	
    59	After an interrupt or a stop of the process, first read what is on disk, as the `fortress-repo` skill's session part says. A stop of the process also keeps the session ID and each Workflow run's journal.
    60	
    61	- Resume a Workflow run. Do not relaunch it. Give the same script and the same arguments, byte for byte, with `resumeFromRunId`, the Workflow tool's argument that names the run to resume.
    62	- At a resume, every agent that had finished keeps its result. An unfinished agent runs again from its start and finds its tree's leftovers. A relaunch would start every agent again.
    63	- A run can be resumed only in the session that launched it: `resumeFromRunId` does not work from a new session. A run that a later resume was meant to extend cannot be finished from a new session. So write a pipeline whole into one script.
    64	
    65	### Matching the launched run exactly
    66	
    67	- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's `agent()` calls, in call order. It misses from the first changed call: that call and the calls after it run live.
    68	- A base given as a short hash, where the launch gave the full hash, misses from the first call.
    69	- If cached calls resolve at once, a script that starts calls as others finish can issue them in another order than the live run did. The resume then misses from that call.
    70	- If the script changed since the launch, resume from a copy of the script as launched: `git show <commit>:<path>`. The Workflow harness also keeps each launched script as `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/workflows/scripts/<name>-<run>.js`.
    71	- If the call order would differ, use a copy that wraps `agent()`, so that the copy issues the finished calls in the journal's order of their `started` lines. Do not change the prompts.
    72	- A copy that changes only what follows the cached prefix runs the changed call live, and nothing before it. A changed prompt is a new key, so that call runs live.
    73	- An agent killed mid-work leaves its edits in its tree, uncommitted, and any staged state. Before the resume, either name them in that agent's prompt, so that the live call checks and keeps them, or stash them and move them aside, so that the call starts clean.
    74	
    75	### The journal
    76	
    77	The journal is `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/journal.jsonl`. It holds one `launched` line, a `started` line for each agent call (`key`, `agentId`, `label`, `phase`), and a `result` line with the same key for each agent that returned. A resume appends to it. If a call runs live again under a key that the journal holds, the call gets a second `started` line. `explorations/coordinator/tools/journal-text.py` reads the journal. The agents' transcripts are the `agent-*.jsonl` files beside it.
    78	
    79	## Continuing or relaunching an Agent-tool worker
    80	
    81	- If a stop of the process stopped the worker, continue it from its transcript with `SendMessage`.
    82	- If an interrupt killed the worker, it cannot be resumed: `SendMessage` is refused. Relaunch it only at the curator's explicit ask.
    83	- Tell the new worker what its predecessor left in the tree. Do not give it the predecessor's transcript: the safety filter has ended a worker that was told to print a predecessor's transcript.
